book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: Tracing the Data Behind a Tool
title: Tracing the Data Behind a Tool
answer: Tracing the data behind an AI tool means teaching students to ask where a tool's information came from and what that origin implies about how the tool behaves. It matters because students can evaluate and use AI well without learning to code, and even young children, who tend to overestimate how intelligent AI agents are, can begin to understand that machines learn from data.

sections.body: This idea is a way of building AI literacy by having students follow a tool back to its data rather than treating the tool as a mysterious or self-directed intelligence. It solves the problem that students, especially young ones, may assume AI agents know things on their own instead of reflecting patterns in data they were given. The approach rests on a definition of AI literacy as the competencies people need to evaluate AI, work with it, and use it well, a definition that does not require coding as a prerequisite. It also gives teachers a planning structure through four aspects of AI literacy: knowing and understanding AI, using and applying it, evaluating and creating with it, and considering its ethics. Tracing data fits naturally into that structure because it turns an abstract question about machine intelligence into something students can investigate.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a teacher plans a unit in which students trace where a tool's data came from and what that means, using the four aspects of AI literacy as a map across grade bands. Younger students concentrate on knowing and understanding AI and on using and applying it, which suits teaching them that machines learn from data. Older students move toward evaluating tools and debating their use, which is where tracing data sources and questioning a tool's outputs becomes central. The book presents Figure 8.6 as the mapping of these aspects to grade bands, so teachers can see which emphasis belongs where. Schools running such units are also advised to build in a simple before and after check of what students learned.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this work as largely untested for learning results. It cites Long and Magerko, 2020, whose review of 150 sources defined AI literacy as competencies for evaluating, working with, and using AI well, and found that coding is not a prerequisite; the same researchers noted that children under about 8 tend to overestimate how intelligent AI agents are. It cites Ng et al., 2021, whose review proposed the four aspects of AI literacy, with Figure 8.6 mapping them to grade bands. It also cites Casal-Otero et al., 2023, a review of 179 documents on AI literacy in schools, which found that few checked whether students actually learned what was taught. Because of that gap, the book recommends that schools build in a simple before and after check so local evidence can improve the unit and add to what the field knows.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit the book sets is that much of this work has not yet been tested for learning results, so teachers should not assume a unit works simply because it is well designed. The decision to run a before and after check stays with the school, and that local evidence is what should guide improvement of the unit. The choice of which aspects of AI literacy to emphasize at each grade band stays with the teacher, guided by the mapping in Figure 8.6 rather than by a fixed rule. Debating the use of AI tools, which the book places with older students, remains a matter for teacher judgment about what a class is ready to discuss. Nothing in the text removes these decisions from people or hands them to the tool itself.
